cards.title: The Three-Question Copy Test (Visualize / Falsify / Distinct)
cards.summary: Run every product headline, ad line and PDP hook through three binary questions to find memorable, credible, ownable copy.
cards.use_when: You are writing or reviewing a product title, ad headline, PDP hero line, email subject or landing page hook and need a fast filter before shipping.
steps: Ask question one: 'Can I visualize it?' Close your eyes and try to picture the words. If nothing concrete appears, the line will not be remembered — cut or rewrite it.

Ask question two: 'Can I falsify it?' If the claim can only be judged as mush (e.g. 'great quality', 'better way'), it reads as filler. Aim for claims that are plainly true-or-false and can be proven.
Ask question three: 'Can nobody else say this?' If a rival store could paste your line onto their page unchanged, it is not positioning. Push until the line is bespoke to your product's facts.
Score: the source treats three 'no' answers as a signal you have written rubbish, and three 'yes' answers as a signal you are onto something. Review the copy line by line, not the whole ad.

Pair the test with the 'One Mississippi, Two Mississippi' speed check: show the creative to another person and if they don't 'get it' within about two seconds of reading, it is too slow for a feed or billboard context.
Keep scores as a personal screen, not a published benchmark — the source gives no data on conversion lift from passing the test.
caveats: A line can be visually concrete and falsifiable yet still irrelevant to purchase motivation; the test screens memorability and ownability, not demand.
Source's claim that 'if everyone gets it, you may be doing something wrong' is an opinion. Confusing the out-crowd can also simply lose sales — decide per audience.
The two-second read threshold is a presenter's heuristic, not a measured conversion rule.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Abstract-to-Concrete Zoom-In Exercise
cards.summary: Rewrite vague benefits by drilling down a two-column abstract/concrete sheet until you hit a picturable object or scenario.
cards.use_when: Your product benefits read as adjectives ('effective', 'convenient', 'premium') and you need concrete claims for ads, PDP bullets or category positioning.
steps: Take a sheet of paper and draw a vertical line down the middle. Write 'abstract' at the top of the left column and 'concrete' at the bottom of the right.
Write your current vague phrase in the left column (e.g. 'regain fitness', 'pretty people in big cities').
Ask repeatedly, 'What do I actually mean here?' and rewrite the phrase lower and lower in the right column, converting intangible words into objects, people, places or actions a reader can picture.
Worked example from the source: 'regain fitness' becomes 'getting people up off the couch to run 5K' — the source notes this is effectively the Couch to 5K naming logic.
Second worked example: 'worn by pretty people in big cities and old people elsewhere' becomes 'worn by supermodels in London and dads in Ohio' — two picturable people in a funny juxtaposition.
Use the resulting concrete phrasing directly as product name, headline or PDP bullet candidates, then run the three-question copy test on each.

Sharpen concrete words further where possible: source critique of a Tesla line suggested preferring 'tougher than an F-150' over 'better truck than an F-150' for shorter, more picturable, more ownable phrasing.
caveats: Drilling down takes real work and multiple rewrites; the source notes 'you can't just like' produce facts — research is required.
Concrete wording can be less searchable or less category-obvious; you may need one concrete emotional line plus one plain functional line on the same PDP.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: 'You Can't Talk, Only Point' — Replace Adjectives With Proof
cards.summary: Write copy by pointing at provable things (charts, objects, people, numbers) instead of using subjective adjectives.
cards.use_when: Your product page or ad is adjective-heavy ('high-quality', 'innovative') and you need provable claims, proof points or image directions.
steps: Set the constraint: describe the product using only statements that are objectively true or false — no 'good-looking', 'trustworthy', 'premium'.
Convert each adjective into a pointed fact. Source dating-app example: replace 'intelligent' with 'reads on the tube'; replace 'good-looking' with 'looks like Ryan Gosling, 6 foot 2'.
For a store context: replace 'durable' with a pointed artifact — a test result, a materials spec, a photo of the seam, a 50-year price chart, or the number of units returned.
Ask for each claim: which object, image or graph can I physically point at that makes this true? If none exists, the claim is wallpaper and should be cut or researched.

The source's gold example: instead of saying gold 'never goes out of fashion', point at the 50-year gold price chart, a castle, a family's gold stash, or Warren Buffett's portfolio allocation — then research which pointed fact actually motivates the buyer.
Translate pointed facts into visual and copy direction on the same PDP or ad unit so text and image reinforce each other.
caveats: Pointing at facts takes research effort; the source explicitly says it 'takes work — that's why it's better', so budget time before publishing.
Some pointed facts are true but unpersuasive ('350 million Americans'); choose facts that carry a story or tension.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Write Claims a Competitor Couldn't Sign
cards.summary: Distinctiveness test: reject any line a competitor could legitimately copy and force copy back to your product's unique facts.
cards.use_when: Your product is functionally similar to competitors (appliances, supplements, apparel) and you need positioning language that separates you in ads and merchandising.
steps: Draft the line, then ask: if a competitor pasted this onto their site, would it still be true for them? If yes, it fails. Credit the principle to Jim Durkey as cited by the source: never write an ad a competitor can sign.
When a line fails, return to product research rather than adjectives. Look for a fact only your product can state — a spec, history, founder story, user base or supply-chain detail.
Source example: Volvo's speedometer ad counts five dials on a rival's speedometer versus six on Volvo's — a fact only Volvo can point at, and a visual that aligns with the text.
Source example: Corvette's 'They don't write songs about Volvos' works because only Corvette can claim that songs (Post Malone, country music) reference Corvettes.
Source example: 'It takes 3.1 seconds to read this ad, the same time it takes a Model S to go 0-60' — a precise, falsifiable, product-specific fact that doubles as a reading-speed gag.
Apply the same exercise to category marketing: source cites Hinge's 'the dating app designed to be deleted', a line a rival dating app can't claim without contradicting its own retention model.
Use whatever survives as the hero line on the PDP, product ad or landing page; keep the plain functional description elsewhere for shoppers who need the category basics.
caveats: Distinctive lines can alienate the out-crowd; the source argues partial confusion is acceptable because it draws attention, but this is a judgement call for your audience size.
Do not invent brand facts to make a line distinctive — the distinctiveness has to come from something true about your product.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Facts First: Ground Every Ad In A Verifiable Fact
cards.summary: Start from a checkable fact (not a number by definition) and build the ad or PDP story from it.
cards.use_when: Your creative or product page feels like opinion, hype or wallpaper and you need a truthful anchor with an internal story.
steps: Locate the fact behind the claim — a spec, a consumption stat, a count, a sourcing detail, a history detail, or a documented behaviour. The source: 'when you say a fact, it guarantees you say something'.
Test the fact's interest level. Source says '350 million Americans' is true but not interesting; find the fact that has a story inside it.
Worked example: 'Asana spends around £345 million a year on sales and marketing' or 'Jack Kerouac wrote On the Road in three weeks' — facts that naturally raise a follow-up question.
Worked example: East-coast-to-London is a six-hour flight — too short to sleep, too long to be quick, which reframes the routine flight misery as a concrete argument.
Worked example: a fast-food worker pours factory ketchup into a Heinz bottle — a fact; the ad line 'even when it's not Heinz, it's Heinz' is built on top of the fact, not the reverse.
Apply to ads and PDPs by starting the copy draft with a facts list for the product, then finding the fact that carries the strongest story and leading with it.
For product claims on PDPs, pair the fact with a visual: chart, photo, spec table or diagram, so the fact is pointable rather than stated.
caveats: The source's dialogue presenters disagree on whether facts are inherently dry — this is a craft opinion. Facts need to carry tension, not just be accurate.
Verify any factual claim before publishing; the source gives sports, business and travel examples as illustrations, not as vetted evidence for your category.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: The Who-Who-Says-What-Well Framework For Copy Briefs
cards.summary: Structure any copy task as: who you're talking to, what you have to say, and saying it well — with visual context driving the format.
cards.use_when: You are briefing a designer, freelancer or yourself before writing an ad, email, PDP hero block or landing page and need to avoid vague inputs.
steps: Point A to Point B: define the buyer's current attitude and the desired attitude after reading, drawing on John Henley's line that the current attitude is the starting point and the desired attitude the finish line. Sketch the wire between them.

Piece 1 — Who you're talking to. Name the channel and moment: a person scrolling a feed, someone who has used your app for months without upgrading, a tourist on a street with a coffee in mind. Source example: Snapchat's Super Bowl ad targeted a moment an average 39-year-old viewer would never occupy.

Piece 2 — What you have to say. For product launches, this means having a belief or 'why' behind the product (the source cites the subscription-economy thesis behind Zuora as an example), so the copy carries a point of view rather than generic benefit lists.

Piece 3 — Say it well. The catchy phrase comes last; the brief must contain pieces 1 and 2 first. Source example: the Hinge brief would be 'an app for people who want long-term relationships and are fed up with dating apps' — the writer then turns that into 'the dating app designed to be deleted'.

Compress into a one-line format reminder: source offers 'coffee and pastry = £5' for a tourist walking past versus a 17-item detailed menu for someone already walking in — form follows the moment, not your internal product richness.

For static ads, layer visual hierarchy the way classic print ads do: eye first hits one element, then a second, then the story. The Hinge visual instead of the mascot is cited as an example of image doing the storytelling work.
Before final, put the draft in the context where it will be seen (see adjacent cards on pre-visualising).
caveats: Piece 2 requires an actual point of view; if your product has none, the framework will just produce polished filler.
The Snapchat and coffee-shop examples are the presenter's anecdotes, not measured outcomes.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Build The Ad In Figma, Not In Word — Design And Copy Are One
cards.summary: Write the ad, landing page or newsletter directly in its final visual layout so line breaks, hierarchy and copy are judged as the reader sees them.
cards.use_when: You are producing static ads, a landing page hero, email creative or a newsletter and copy and layout decisions are being made separately.
steps: Choose the live surface as the writing tool: source writes newsletters inside the email platform, ads inside Figma, and would pin a billboard mockup among competing billboards. Never draft in a plain doc for final layout.
Set placeholder images early so the copy is written around the visual shape, in the way source placed two placeholder illustrations before writing final lines.
Judge line breaks: source rewrote a line several times purely because it spilled onto two lines in the layout and looked messy — settle the copy until it fits the intended line count.
Use layout references from classic print ads (source cites a Volkswagen winter-preparation ad with structure to mirror) as models for hierarchy and density.
Iterate with design and wording together; source estimates the worked ad took roughly 2 days and about 25 rewrites.
For static ads, mock it into a feed or billboard context with other ads around it before signing off — the source warns that a clean isolated mockup lies about stopping power.
caveats: Writing in the tool is slower; if the surface is not fixed, at least prototype in the correct aspect ratio before sign-off.
Figma and other tool UIs change — verify current behaviour before enforcing a specific workflow with a team.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Pre-Visualise The Ad In Real Context (Feed, Billboard, Inbox)
cards.summary: Test stopping power by placing the creative where the buyer will actually see it, not against a blank canvas.
cards.use_when: You are approving static ad creatives, email headers or social hooks and want to know whether they grab attention in a busy feed.
steps: After designing the ad, pull it into a mockup with six or seven other ads around it and people walking past (source suggests this is how you'd test a billboard).
Ask: does it actually grab attention against that noise, not against the isolated Figma frame?
Apply the One Mississippi, Two Mississippi speed check to the in-context mockup: if the reader doesn't get it within about two seconds, the hook is too slow for the surface.

For email, write the newsletter directly inside the sending tool (the source uses ConvertKit) rather than in a Google doc, because line lengths shift when pasted and the reader will see the copy wrapped differently to the draft.

For store landing pages, view the hero on mobile in a browser with the surrounding UI and competitor tabs open — this is the ecommerce translation of the source's feed mockup method, not a claim from the source.
Do not skip the context mockup because the isolated design looks tidy — the source explicitly warns against judging a designed-but-isolated ad as if it were a real one.
caveats: A channel that is intentionally niche and only needs to resonate with an in-crowd may fail the two-second test by design; the source accepts this trade-off, though you should weigh it against lost reach.
No conversion benchmark is given; treat the two-second rule as a creative-floor check, not a performance prediction.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Conflict Pairing To Generate Ad Ideas (Sullivan's Line Down The Page)
cards.summary: Brainstorm ad concepts by listing two opposing ideas on either side of a page and writing the argument between them.
cards.use_when: You need a fresh static ad or landing page angle and your current drafts are flat feature lists.
steps: Draw a line down the middle of the page. On one side, write your product's benefit in plain terms — e.g. 'increase landing page conversions from 1% to 2%'.
On the other side, write the natural opposing choice or cost — e.g. 'spend twice as much on ads'.
Read the pair as an argument: which side is the ad opening with, and what does the reader need to hear to accept the second side?

Classify the conflict by enemy type if it helps: A = a different approach to the same problem, B = a belief disagreement, C = a direct competitor. Source uses Volkswagen's winter-preparation ad and Apple's Mac vs PC work as examples of C.
Write the header as a choice between the two sides: source ended up with 'Want to grow twice as fast? You have two choices.'
If the argument feels thin, keep pairing different opposing ideas and read them as arguments rather than as a slogan list.
Bring the resulting pair into design as a layout, leaning on the visual reference you have collected (source cites a Volkswagen ad layout as the template that made the final version work).
caveats: Source treats conflict as a loose brainstorming device — it explicitly says 'I don't take this too seriously, just draw a line and write opposites'. It is a generator, not a formula.
Conflicts that insult a customer segment or misstate the rival's product can backfire and create legal or community risk; keep the conflict factual.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Drafting By 'Bleeding The Ink Dry' — Spitball Then Curate
cards.summary: Generate a large volume of rough candidate lines without judging them, then select and refine down through many rewrites.
cards.use_when: You are stuck on a headline, hook or hero line and every draft you produce is either obvious or precious.
steps: Accept that the final line is almost never written directly. Source: 'I couldn't write that as it is on the screen right now.'
Spitball freely and badly. Source produced lines like 'Go fool Zuckerberg', 'Roll Monopoly dice', 'Hidden hope', 'Spaghetti at war' before arriving at usable material.
Compare it to running a dirty tap: the first output is muddy, and the goal is to keep flowing until it runs clean, without judging each early line.
After a burst of generation, pause and select. Source noted he couldn't tell good from bad after 2-3 hours of work and had to get trusted feedback — use a small group whose taste you respect.
Rewrite repeatedly around constraints (header length, line count, parallelism). Source's final had roughly 25 rewrites across about several days.
Stop when the structure, hierarchy and wording hold up against the visual mockup and pass the three-question copy test — source describes the moment as 'you literally can't' improve further.
Apply the same loop to PDP hero copy and email subject lines: run a batch of bad candidates through a screening pass rather than trying to write one perfect line.
caveats: High-volume iteration needs time budgeted; source spent days, which is impractical for daily ad rotations.
Ego check: source accepts he couldn't judge his own work after long sessions and relies on a small advisory group; without that, review bias can push you to ship weak work.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Build An Argument, Not A Claim — Small Believable Promises
cards.summary: Frame ads as arguments that move the buyer from a current to a desired belief, with modest believable claims rather than big hype.
cards.use_when: You are writing the hero section, email or paid ad for a conversion offer and want the claim to be credible rather than oversized.
steps: Treat copy as argument: the conclusion is the purchase, and the body of the ad is the reasoning.
Choose a claim the reader can plausibly accept. Source's completed ad argues 'learn copywriting' by claiming 'increase landing page conversions from 1% to 2%' rather than 'become a millionaire'.

Use in the argument the natural cost side of the choice: the source pairs learning copywriting against 'raise twice the cash, hire twice the staff, spend twice as much on ads, cross both your fingers'.

Change the frame of the offer so it saves the reader something instead of costing them. Source's other ad reframes '2 hours to learn copywriting' against '22,000 hours of writing over a career', turning a time cost into a time saving.

Amplify a small number by expanding its time frame. Source derives about 22,000 hours from roughly 4 hours a day writing x 300 days a year x a 30-year career — he notes the figures are his working assumptions, not sourced statistics.
Mirror the structure on the live page: place the choice or the argument visibly, not buried, and bold the key terms that carry the logic.
For ecommerce: replace generic 'premium' claims on a PDP with an argued comparison (e.g. cost per use, hours saved, replacements avoided) where the arithmetic is defensible.
caveats: The 22,000-hour figure is a personal estimate constructed with the words 'give or take'; do not present it as verified data for your own category.
Small believable claims are more credible but may be less click-magnetic than aggressive ones; the source prefers sincerity over hype, which is a positioning choice.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Positioning By Replacement And Smarter-Choice Framing
cards.summary: Define the product by what it replaces and by the smart, self-flattering decision it lets the buyer make.
cards.use_when: Your product is one of many similar options or has an obvious cheaper alternative, and you need a positioning line for PDP or ad creative.
steps: Ask 'what does it replace?' Source example: Athletic Greens' 'you're going to need a smaller cabinet' communication positions it as replacing a shelf of vitamins and supplements. In a store context this maps directly to bundle, refill and regimen language.
Point to the pain of the replaced behaviour: source names the morning-routine hassle of vitamin A, C, D, zinc as the pain point the positioning attacks.

Second framing tool: let the buyer feel smart, not just flattered. Source example: 'the sport sedan for people who inherited brains instead of wealth' — the buyer of a modest car is invited to see themselves as financially intelligent.

Source's paraphrase of the underlying principle: if you can make the customer feel like they're making a smart decision, you are doing something right. Attribute this to the source's paraphrase, not a measured result.

Check the framing is defensible: it should be a claim your actual product can support, and provable to the shopper. 'Smarter than buying a Ferrari' works only if you can point to running cost, resale or durability facts.
Use the positioning in the hero and the replacement language in the comparison or bundle block on a PDP — the source illustrates the replacement idea visually with the cabinet image.
Test against the three-question copy test: can the buyer visualize the replacement or the smart choice, is the claim falsifiable, and could a rival store say the same line?
caveats: The source's own caveat on the smarter-choice angle: some ads assume an in-crowd who will 'get it' instantly while others won't. In ecommerce that risks abandonment by a broader cold audience.
No conversion evidence is provided for these framings; treat them as copy hypotheses to test on your PDP or ad set.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: The One-Element Ad — Strip To The Essential Component
cards.summary: Reduce an ad to a single powerful element rather than the default header + subheader + picture + logo, if the single element can carry the message.
cards.use_when: You are designing static ads or PDP hero blocks with too much going on and want to increase stopping power.
steps: Start from the default spec — header, subheader, picture, logo — and then ask whether you can do the ad with just one of those.
Source cites Neil French via the episode: if you can do an ad with just one of those elements, you're onto a winner.

Worked example: the Economist 'I've never read The Economist — management trainee, aged 42' ad has no apparent subheader, no picture, and the logo absent in the standard position; the ad's identity comes from brand colour and the word 'Economist' embedded in the copy.
For ecommerce translation: test a static ad or PDP hero that is one compelling sentence and one visual, or even just one sentence, rather than the standard headline + subhead + CTA stack.
Keep the identification cues the brand owns (colour, distinctive typography, a recognisable phrase) so the stripped ad is still attributed to you, as the source notes for the Economist red.
Sequence is deliberate: the source points to the first line causing a question and the second line resolving it — 'It takes 3.1 seconds to read this ad / the same time it takes a Model S to go 0-60'.
Apply the One Mississippi, Two Mississippi check to the reduced ad before shipping.
caveats: The source's claim that one-element ads are 'a winner' is Neil French's craft opinion relayed by the presenter, not a measured rule.
Reduction can cost clarity for shoppers who scan for price, specification or shipping information; the stripped creative may need a denser supporting block on the same page.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Storytelling With Cultural Scaffolding, Not Mascots
cards.summary: Let imagery lean on shared cultural references the audience already holds instead of inventing mascots that fit an unrelated category tone.
cards.use_when: You are choosing the hero image or creative concept for a brand whose promise is serious and where a mascot or gimmick would clash.
steps: Ask what the audience already knows and feels about this category that the image can rest on. Source describes the Hinge hero image as resting on cultural scaffolding rather than inventing meaning.

Match the tone of the imagery to the emotional seriousness of the promise. The source argues Duolingo-style mascots suit a silly, funny category, while dating-for-marriage content should be real and not silly.

If the existing brand visual is doing the wrong emotional job, replace it. Source's example: he removed a mascot from a landing page he was working on, and considers the replacement image to have told the story better.

Build in the customer's next believed moment: the source reads the Hinge line as implying 'I'll meet someone, live happily ever after, and delete the app' — the image should reinforce that implied outcome, not just the feature.
Reject images that carry no shared reference and require explanation (the source's 'if everyone gets it, you might be doing something wrong' cuts the other way when the audience is cold).
For store landing pages, audit hero imagery for whether it references a customer-known situation (usage moment, occasion, aspiration) or just a fabricated brand prop.
caveats: The Hinge mascot removal and image choice is one practitioner's judgement — it is not an A/B test result.
Cultural scaffolding ages; an image referencing a current meme or celebrity decays quickly and may date the PDP.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Copy As Positioning: The Same Product, Sold Differently
cards.summary: Copy and branding can move identical commodities into completely different sales outcomes by positioning them differently.
cards.use_when: Your product is functionally similar to cheaper alternatives (commodity categories, private label comparisons) and you need a reason to exist beyond features.
steps: Accept the starting point: two physically similar products can differ only by positioning and reputation. Source compares a Snickers bar with a discontinued Fuse bar of similar appearance and taste, one of which reached the world's best-selling chocolate bar status.
Look for the existing positioning line that already owns a moment, before writing more copy. Snickers' 'You're not you when you're hungry' is cited as the example of a line that lands.

When the product itself is weak, shift the angle rather than improve the product. Source cites footballer Dave Kitson, who outsold Beckham, Lampard, Gerrard and Owen books by reframing marginal playing career material as behind-the-scenes Premier League exposé, released anonymously as The Secret Footballer.
The rule the source extracts from the Kitson story: ask 'what can I do that no one else is doing that people care about?'

Translate to ecommerce: for a functional commodity, find a credibly distinct angle — an access story, a supply-chain confession, an unusual usage occasion, a founder position — and write it into the PDP and ads, rather than adding adjective preambles.

Pair with brand-level positioning references the source uses, such as Ogilvy's 'we don't choose the whiskey, we choose the image' and 17 of 20 American teenagers choosing Apple — reminders that choice reasons sit outside the spec sheet.
Re-verify the copy against the three-question test once the angle is chosen.
caveats: Some of the source's material is presenter anecdote ('I think it's an example of a foundational principle'); the Snickers/Fuse comparison and the Kitson outcome are illustrations, not controlled evidence.
Positioning stories that lean on secrecy or consumer deception carry reputational risk; if adapting the Secret Footballer pattern, keep claims true and defensible.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Metonymy — Swap Literal Category Words For Visual Ones
cards.summary: Replace a literal category label in copy with a concrete, surprising stand-in that is more visual and memorable.
cards.use_when: Your PDP or ad copy uses category words ('device', 'subscription plan', 'storage') that read flat and you need a line that sticks.
steps: Identify the literal, correct word the copy is actually describing. Source example: what Apple really meant was '1,000 songs in your media player'.
Choose a stand-in that a reader can picture instead. Source substitutes 'pocket' — the ad becomes '1,000 songs in your pocket'.

Accept the deliberate imprecision: the source acknowledges the sentence doesn't literally make sense, and treats that as the point — 'pocket' is more visual, surprising and punchy than 'media player'.
Check what the swap does to the claim: it should sharpen imagery, not misstate what the product does, or create a claim you cannot substantiate on the PDP.
Use for hero lines, packaging-adjacent copy and ad headlines where brevity matters; keep the literal description available in specs or FAQs for shoppers who need it.

Test the substitute against the three-question copy test, and consider whether the substituted term itself is one a competitor could also use — the standing-in word should ideally feel owned by your brand.
caveats: The source treats metonymy as a technique, not a rule for every line — it's easy to push into nonsense if the stand-in word is not instantly picturable.
Product-page legal and factual copy may not tolerate substitution; keep the visual line and the literal spec separate.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: Contrast and Juxtaposition As The Engine Of Memorability
cards.summary: Build memorable lines by putting two opposing ideas, numbers or images side by side and letting the tension do the work.
cards.use_when: You are writing a headline, subject line or hero copy and want it to stick without hype.
steps: Look for a pairing that creates a small tension. Source examples: 'supermodels in London and dads in Ohio'; 'tougher than an F-150, faster than a Porsche 911'.

In the De Beers example cited by the source, the line is 'how can you make two months' salary last forever?' — the source notes the line 'shouldn't work' because two months' salary and forever are in direct contradiction, which is why it sticks.
Where the numbers are involved, make the contrast do arithmetic or logic work: source's 'the difference between 1% and 2% is not just 1%, it's 100%' framed the whole ad's argument.
Structure an ad around the contrast as a two-option choice: source's finished ad sets 'throw money and pray' against 'learn copywriting', in parallel items.
Keep the two sides parallel in rhythm and word count where possible. Source highlights the repetition of 'twice' and 'both' across parallel lines as something worth pulling out with bolding.
For a store, apply this when a product is premium, cheaper-per-use, or has a surprising comparison: put the two numbers or outcomes side by side in hero and comparison blocks.
Verify both sides of the contrast are true on your PDP; the De Beers line works because the two sides are both real in the campaign, not because of wordplay alone.
caveats: Contrasts that drift into exaggeration break the falsifiable test and can invite complaints or platform flags.
The 'difference is 100%' framing is an argument about relative improvement, not a claim that every 1% lift yields doubled growth — source presents it as a copywriting argument, not a growth model.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: If Possible: Publish Sourced Feedback Loops In Ad Production
cards.summary: Route finished ad copy through a small circle of trusted-taste reviewers before shipping, especially after long drafting sessions.
cards.use_when: You have been writing the same ad, subject line or hero for hours and can't judge whether it's good; you have trusted colleagues or peers available.
steps: Recognise the moment: source says after 2-3 hours of writing he cannot tell what is good and what is not, and reaches out.
Send the candidate to a small group whose taste you respect, not an open pool — source sent the draft to a handful of people.

Give them the candidates side by side with the alternatives. In the source example, the options included 'Go fool Zuckerberg', 'the corporate way' and 'throw money and pray', and the feedback settled on 'throw money and pray' as the left header.
Treat feedback as signal on taste and clarity, not as a vote on raw ideas — the source kept elements from the rejected options elsewhere in the layout.
Feed the result into the next iteration, then run the same reviewers past the revised version if the structure changed materially.
For ecommerce, apply this to PDP hero and email subject lines where one-word or one-line differences swing click-through; keep the reviewing circle small and consistent.
caveats: Source's reviewers are chosen for taste, not statistical representativeness — their verdicts are not consumer research.
Do not outsource final judgement entirely; the source keeps working after feedback receives the verdict, and note that some channels may not have a reviewing circle at all.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx
